claims.text: A MoNbTaW-based refractory high-entropy alloy can exhibit superconductivity at cryogenic temperatures after minor compositional adjustments.
The proposed superconductivity arises from enhanced electron–phonon coupling in a disordered BCC lattice.
The starting material is a nanocrystalline or polycrystalline refractory HEA containing Mo, Nb, Ta, and W.
The starting MoNbTaW-based HEA has a largely disordered BCC structure.
The starting alloy can be processed by spark plasma sintering or laser powder bed fusion.
Small changes in the relative Mo, Nb, Ta, and W concentrations can tune the alloy toward superconductivity.
A combined experimental and simulation methodology can be used to design and assess refractory HEAs.
Scanning tunneling spectroscopy and first-principles calculations can determine the superconducting gap and electron–phonon coupling of the proposed alloy.
Cryogenic measurements under controlled magnetic fields can identify superconducting transitions and critical parameters.
The proposed HEA has high configurational entropy.
Randomly distributed constituent elements with different atomic radii produce intrinsic lattice distortions in HEAs.
Configurational entropy and BCC lattice distortions modify the electronic density of states and phonon spectra.
Disorder in the lattice enhances electron–phonon coupling.
Enhanced electron–phonon coupling facilitates Cooper-pair formation and the onset of superconductivity.
The alloy is expected to show both zero electrical resistance and a Meissner effect.
Its critical temperature may be comparable to or modestly lower than that of conventional superconductors.
The HEA may have improved mechanical robustness.
Compositional inhomogeneity, excessive disorder, or processing-induced phase decomposition may suppress superconductivity.
The superconducting critical temperature and gap depend on a complex interplay between chemical disorder and electron–phonon interactions.
